quarterly_data.signal: CALL — DECEMBER 2025 QUARTER RESULTS AND MIX: CFO Doug Bettinger said December-quarter revenue was a record $5.34 billion, Lam's tenth consecutive quarter of revenue growth and above the guidance midpoint; non-GAAP gross margin 49.7%, operating margin 34.3% and diluted EPS $1.27 all beat the high end of guidance. Calendar 2025: record revenue of $20.6 billion (up 27% year over year), record CSBG revenue of $7.2 billion, gross margin 49.9%, record operating margin 34.1%, diluted EPS $4.89. Deferred revenue ended at $2.25 billion, down sequentially on an approximately $500 million reduction in customer advance down payments. Mix: foundry was 59% of systems revenue (slightly down sequentially but up from 35% in the December 2024 quarter), driven by leading-edge investment plus mature-node spending in China; memory was 34%. Regions: China 35% of revenue (down from 43%, but slightly above plan because affiliate-rule updates shifted shipment timing), Taiwan 20% (from 19%), Korea 20% (from 15%). Outlook: management sees China WFE 'flattish' from 2025 to 2026 while everything else grows, so China's share of Lam revenue should drop to somewhere in the 'low thirties or high twenties'.
quarterly_data.figure: Dec-qtr revenue record $5.34 billion; GM 49.7%, OM 34.3%, EPS $1.27; CY2025 revenue $20.6 billion (+27%), CSBG $7.2 billion; foundry 59% of systems revenue (35% a year earlier); China 35% of revenue (from 43%), Taiwan 20%, Korea 20%

quarterly_data.signal: CALL — MARCH 2026 QUARTER GUIDE AND SHAPE OF 2026 (non-GAAP): revenue $5.7 billion plus or minus $300 million; gross margin 49%, plus or minus one percentage point, with slight customer-mix headwinds ('It's going to be less rich in the March quarter'); operating margin 34% plus or minus one percentage point; EPS $1.35 plus or minus $0.10 on approximately 1.26 billion shares. Bettinger expects 'growth every quarter' (March, then June, then September), so 2026 will be 'a second half weighted year both from a WP standpoint and from our revenue'. CEO Tim Archer added that 'basically every customer is asking for pull ins'. Management said Lam will 'outperform WFE this year', is already running ahead of its Investor Day long-term model and will likely update that model later in the year. CSBG should keep growing 'kinda high single digit, maybe low double digit'.
quarterly_data.figure: Mar-qtr guide: revenue $5.7 billion plus or minus $300 million; GM 49%; OM 34%; EPS $1.35 plus or minus $0.10

quarterly_data.signal: CALL — FIRST CY2026 WFE VIEW, LIMITED BY CLEAN-ROOM SPACE: Archer said 2025 WFE came in close to $110 billion and Lam's initial 2026 view is 'in the $135 billion range', with 'the growth in spending remaining constrained by a shortage of available clean room space'. He expects WFE to be weighted to the second half, with growth in all three device segments 'led by DRAM and leading-edge foundry logic'. Bettinger declined to put a number on how much WFE the constraint costs ('plans are somewhat fluid'). He said 'the industry seems to be sold out for most of what it's supplying', that customers are working on multiyear agreements, and that this 'sets up for '27 to also be a pretty good year'. Archer said the many announced fabs add capacity in '27, '28 and beyond, so the constraints should last until those fabs open, and that visibility into the following year is the best he 'can ever remember'. Share: Lam's SAM share of WFE reached the mid-thirties percent range (multiyear goal: high thirties), its ship share grew by well over one percentage point, 2025 share gains came from 'a combination of both NAND and foundry logic', and Lam plans 'to increase our share of WFE again this year'. Lam itself is 'not the big constraint': its supply chain is broader and deeper than during the post-COVID shortages, and it sees no significant supplier problems ahead.
quarterly_data.figure: CY2026 WFE initial view $135 billion range (2025 WFE close to $110 billion); clean-room constrained, second-half weighted; SAM share mid-thirties percent

quarterly_data.signal: CALL — GATE-ALL-AROUND AND AKARA: Archer said foundry-logic customers are 'accelerating migration to nodes employing gate-all-around', a transition worth 'roughly $1 billion in incremental Lam Sam for every 100,000 wafer starts per month of capacity'. Akara, Lam's latest-generation conductor etch system (printed 'Aqara'/'Acara' in this transcript), doubled its installed base over the past year and won production tool-of-record positions for EUV and high-aspect-ratio etch in advanced DRAM and foundry logic. Critical dimensions in foundry logic shrink roughly 10 to 20% node to node, and in next-generation gate-all-around devices the number of applications using Akara should grow by roughly two times, including critical front-end silicon etch. Drivers still ahead: 'Backside power is still to come, and it's gonna be a driver for us', along with the later move to CFET and more advanced packaging across leading-edge foundry at future nodes. Lam has refreshed its conductor and dielectric etch lines and launched Moly.
quarterly_data.figure: GAA = roughly $1 billion incremental SAM per 100,000 wafer starts per month; Akara installed base doubled; Akara applications roughly two times in next-gen GAA; CDs shrink roughly 10 to 20% per node

quarterly_data.signal: CALL — ADVANCED PACKAGING TO GROW MORE THAN 40%: Archer expects Lam's overall advanced packaging business 'to grow more than 40% in 2026, outperforming our view of WFE growth in this space'. Lam had previously estimated advanced packaging at a mid-single-digit percentage of foundry-logic equipment spend, and Archer now sees that share rising as more devices, including mobile, adopt more complex packaging schemes. He cited Lam's market leadership in electroplating and TSV etch (printed 'TSC etch'). The growth figure covers both HBM and more complex packaging in advanced foundry logic ('we've lumped it together'), and Lam's copper plating, etch and dielectric gap-fill tools are used to package all device types. In some cases customers have shifted clean-room space toward advanced packaging. Bettinger would not size 2025 packaging revenue beyond saying 'it grew nicely'.
quarterly_data.figure: advanced packaging business to grow more than 40% in 2026

quarterly_data.signal: CALL — LAM'S OWN CAPACITY BUILD: Lam has nearly doubled its overall manufacturing capacity over the last four years. Malaysia is now its biggest location, alongside factories in Oregon, California, Ohio, Taiwan, Korea and Austria. Lam launched automated warehouses in 2025 and bought a new building in Arizona to support the growing industry footprint there. December-quarter capex was $261 million (up $76 million sequentially), spent on manufacturing capacity, R&D and lab infrastructure, and capex should stay in the 4% to 5% of revenue range. Lam expects to build inventory in dollar terms ahead of a growing top line. The Customer Support Business Group brought in approximately $2 billion of revenue in the December quarter, up 12% sequentially on Reliant systems (demand from both multinationals and China). The installed base topped 100,000 chambers, and Dextro cobots expanded to six Lam tool types in 2025.
quarterly_data.figure: Dec-qtr capex $261 million; capex 4% to 5% of revenue; CSBG approximately $2 billion (up 12% sequentially); installed base topping 100,000 chambers; manufacturing capacity nearly doubled over four years

players.product: etch and deep-silicon-via TSV etch systems

quarterly_data.signal: CALL — RECORD DRAM, HBM3E/HBM4 SPENDING: memory was 34% of December-quarter systems revenue, and record DRAM revenue made up 23% of systems revenue (up from 16% in the September quarter). Bettinger said 'Investments in high bandwidth memory continued to remain strong, driven by movement to HBM3e and four', and node migrations to 1B and 1C are enabling the DDR5 transition. Archer said advanced packaging is critical for the move to HBM4 and 4E (printed 'HVM four and four e') and stacking of up to 16 layers, where Lam leads in electroplating and TSV etch. Asked about HBM4 with 16 layers, Archer said next-generation HBM dies 'become bigger', which is the main cause of the clean-room crunch because each generation needs more clean-room space and more tooling for the same output. DRAM and leading-edge foundry logic lead 2026 WFE growth, and memory makers are 'prioritizing DRAM over NAND a little bit because profitability there is somewhat better'.
quarterly_data.figure: record DRAM = 23% of systems revenue (from 16%); memory 34%; HBM stacking of up to 16 layers

quarterly_data.signal: CALL — DRAM ETCH ROADMAP: Lam already has Akara wins (printed 'the car') for the 1C DRAM node that are set to ramp this year, and expects applications using Akara to expand nearly three times at the following node (printed 'one d node'). DRAM aspect ratios increase with each node, and process complexity will grow further with future moves to four f squared (4F2) and 3D DRAM. On 4F2 timing, Archer said customers talk about full volume production 'towards the end of the decade', probably after the next big wave of fab openings, and that Akara suits its high-aspect-ratio, very small features. Moly ALD adoption order: NAND first, then foundry logic, then DRAM.
quarterly_data.figure: Akara DRAM applications to expand nearly three times at the node after 1C; four f squared volume towards the end of the decade

players.product: high-aspect-ratio dielectric etch & cryogenic etch tools for NAND stacks

quarterly_data.signal: CALL — NEW AI-INFERENCE NAND USE CASE: Archer said NAND demand 'is growing faster than previously expected' as new uses for high-capacity SSDs emerge, including non-volatile context memory layers for large-scale AI inference. His estimate: 'For every two to three million accelerators sold, we estimate an incremental one-point increase in overall NAND bit demand growth.' He called this 'a new use case' ('I don't think we saw this particular use case coming'), tied to AI inference and a growing inference cache (printed 'TD cache'). It goes beyond the enterprise-SSD projections Lam gave at its Investor Day a year earlier. Bettinger noted that one of the big accelerator makers said at CES that it needs this NAND. In the December quarter, non-volatile memory was 11% of systems revenue, down from 18% in September, in line with customer plans for a first-half-weighted 2025. NAND spending still drove record 2025 upgrade revenue, up more than 90% year over year. Lam has the industry's largest installed base of NAND systems.
quarterly_data.figure: every two to three million accelerators sold = one-point increase in NAND bit demand growth; NVM 11% of systems revenue (from 18%); 2025 upgrade revenue up more than 90%

quarterly_data.signal: CALL — NAND UPGRADES FIRST, GREENFIELD LATER: Bettinger said 2026 'will be a growth year for NAND', probably 'a little bit second half weighted'. He expects upgrades to come before real capacity additions and said the 40 billion upgrade opportunity 'likely happens quicker than what we originally expected a year ago'. One of Lam's largest customers has announced a new fab heavily weighted toward NAND capacity. Archer said clean-room limits probably push large greenfield NAND additions into the multiyear '27-'28 build-out. Until then customers are speeding up technology transitions to get more high-performance bits, so Lam is 'busy doing upgrades'. Lam may update the 40 billion figure later in the year as NAND's role in AI inference grows. On Moly ALD, NAND is adopting first, and the customers that have committed to production with Moly in NAND have chosen Lam's tools (printed 'LAN's tools'). Archer said Lam's single-wafer, multi-station Moly tool is the industry's production tool of choice. Lam also gained NAND share in 2025 on new applications needed for higher layer counts.
quarterly_data.figure: 40 billion NAND upgrade opportunity happening quicker than expected; greenfield later in the multiyear build-out; 2026 a growth year for NAND
